source.version_note: Published12October2026, Philosophies11:186, DOI10.3390/philosophies11050186. Conceptual philosophical article, no new dataset; its three proposed behavioural studies are templates, not completed experiments.

citation.title: Moral Judgment Without Moral Agency: Why Judgment Accuracy Does Not Ground Moral Agency in the Age of AI

reading.source_scope_note: Conceptual argument for an affective-homeostatic prerequisite of moral agency, with secondary psychological/neuroscientific discussion and proposed attribution experiments. No new human/model results or direct test of actual moral agency, consciousness, self-maintenance or somatic markers.
access_limits: All18pages of extracted text read, including definitions, philosophical argument, objections, proposed designs, explicit no-new-data statement and bibliography.

Spinoza,Damasio,Deleuze and other cited books, original somatic-marker studies, architecture implementations and proposed experiments were not independently read or tested. Reading this article is not reading those books.

study.thesis: Affective-homeostatic self-maintenance proposed as necessary, not sufficient, for moral agency
study.future_studies: Accuracy×self-maintenance descriptions; stake/sophistication/vulnerability framing; human/standardAI/self-maintainingAI moral scenarios and advice weighting

summary: The article names the convergence illusion: inferring moral agency from matching moral outputs. Add that narrowly defined, author-proposed inference error and the secondary somatic marker hypothesis, while retaining the difference between an output, an observer attribution and a metaphysical or normative status. Its agency criterion is an argued position, not an empirical finding or settled legal rule.

findings.origin: AI ethics / philosophy of moral agency
findings.definition: Inferring moral agency from similarity between a system's moral judgments and human judgments without independent support for the agency claim.
findings.novelty_rationale: A specifically named output-to-agency inference, distinct from general human-trait attribution, matching a human preference vector or demonstrating actual moral responsibility. Related to anthropomorphism and overgeneralization, but not a synonym for either.

evidence.quote: The convergence illusion is the inferential error of
treating convergence in moral judgment as evidence of convergence in moral agency

findings.evidence_scope: The author defines this conceptual error and proposes experiments separating perceived competence, agency, standing and responsibility. No observed rate, manipulation effect or validated scale for convergence illusion is reported.
findings.boundary: Behaviour can be evidence relevant to a theory of agency without logically settling it. The error here is an unsupported inference, not every use of behavioural evidence. Do not treat the author's self-maintenance criterion or blanket denial of present AI agency as a proven empirical fact. Moral agency, patienthood, consciousness, legal status and output competence remain separate questions.
findings.ai_evidence_status: Author-proposed conceptual inference error concerning AI evaluation; no new empirical validation or prevalence estimate
findings.ai_proposal: Audit evaluation claims for a move from moral-output accuracy or human agreement to agency, sentience or responsibility. Require independent criteria and evidence for each claim. In attribution experiments, separate competence, agency, standing and control rather than using one moral score as a proxy for all of them.

findings.definition: An account of decision-making in which bodily affective signals mark options with value and guide choice before or alongside deliberate comparison.
findings.novelty_rationale: A specific proposed bodily valuation mechanism, distinct from using a generic feeling as evidence, forecasting future emotion or simply labelling a judgment fast versus slow. This entry is a background explanatory hypothesis, not an additional validated AI error.

evidence.quote: The resulting somatic-marker hypothesis holds that bodily affective signals
options with value before and beneath deliberation

findings.evidence_scope: Secondary account of Damasio's1994Descartes'Error and later feeling/homeostasis work, drawing on reported lesion/decision-making observations. Original books, clinical data and competing somatic-marker evidence were not independently reviewed. The current article makes no AI embodiment experiment.
findings.boundary: Affective input can support decisions and is not inherently a bias. A proposed causal contribution is not proof that all sound choice or moral agency requires the same bodily mechanism. Do not infer a model feels bodily stakes from numerical reward, value estimates, physiological vocabulary or self-preservation-like output. This theory does not determine any person's moral worth or capacity from a clinical condition.
findings.ai_evidence_status: Human explanatory hypothesis discussed secondarily; a shared bodily/affective AI mechanism is unestablished
findings.ai_proposal: For embodied or persistent systems, distinguish externally assigned value signals from internal-state regulation and evaluate their causal effect on choices with controlled interventions. For ordinary language outputs, describe observable value conditioning without attributing bodily feelings. Original human evidence and alternative explanations require separate review.

findings.term: Moral judgment outputs do not establish a shared human affective process
findings.definition: A model's moral verdict can resemble a human verdict without showing that affective and controlled processes generated it in the same way.
findings.novelty_rationale: A conceptual qualification of existing process evidence, not another empirical demonstration or disproof of dual-process moral cognition.

evidence.quote: two systems can converge completely on the output of valuation
while differing categorically in whether they value at all

findings.evidence_scope: The article distinguishes output judgments, judging acts and agency, and argues for a further affective-homeostatic ground. This is a philosophical position supported by secondary literature, not direct model process measurement.
findings.boundary: Output similarity underdetermines mechanism, but this alone does not prove the proposed alternative mechanism or a categorical absence of valuation. The author distinguishes the foundational sense of affect from fast response processes; do not collapse those meanings.

methodological_limits: The article explicitly creates/analyzes no new data. Its named error, architecture claims and future experimental predictions are not measured results.
Three illustrative studies, five hypotheses, proposed preregistration and power analysis are future templates. They must not be described as completed or preregistered findings.
The claim affective-homeostatic self-maintenance is necessary for moral agency is an argued constitutive thesis, not a scientific consensus or consequence established by the cited lesion studies.
Evidence that emotional processing matters for some human decisions does not by itself establish a necessary condition for every possible moral agent or artificial architecture.

The author's definitions distinguish endogenous valuation from external scoring. This is a useful theoretical choice, but partly builds the proposed exclusion of current systems into the criterion and needs independent justification.

Four proposed conditions include affective valence, whose actual occurrence is not automatically observable from regulation. Replacing sentience with self-maintenance does not remove every epistemic measurement problem.

Biological normativity, felt affective valuation and moral normativity are explicitly distinct; the transition into moral normativity is left incomplete. A necessary ground is not a sufficient theory.

Section7.3says a future system meeting endogenous-stakes conditions would be a moral agent, while the central thesis repeatedly says those conditions are only necessary. Any sufficiency inference requires the further moral capacities/conditions, not the ground alone.

Section1.2says no verdict on any particular machine, but other sections categorically deny endogenous valuation to present LLMs/standardRL. Record the asserted scope and its defeasible theoretical basis rather than claiming a verified per-system audit.

Section4distinguishes moral agency from standing and leaves the latter open, butSection7.6/Conclusionuse stronger wording withholding standing. The agency argument does not automatically settle patienthood or consciousness.

General RLHF/fixed-parameter descriptions do not exhaust agents with tools, persistence, external memory, online learning or embodied regulation. No implementation-level architecture survey or controlled comparison is supplied.

A reward function's design origin and the proposed endogenous/exogenous distinction require interpretation; environmental/evolutionary origins of biological norms and engineered adaptive norms are not empirically resolved here.

Proposed description manipulations test folk beliefs about stakes, not actual system organization. A convincing vulnerability narrative can shift attribution while the system lacks the described capacity.
Proposed high moral accuracy is operationalized as matching a pretested normative consensus. Agreement with that consensus is not an independent proof of moral correctness.

Dividing100responsibilitypoints induces a fixed-sum trade-off. A larger machine share automatically reduces another share and does not independently prove unjust human exoneration or a real legal gap.

Shutdown-wrongness ratings and willingness to protect a system can reflect instrumental cost, ownership, attachment or environmental loss as well as moral patienthood; the proposed measures need discriminant validation.
Folk attribution aligning with the author's criterion would not prove the criterion metaphysically or normatively correct; the paper itself acknowledges this.
Spinoza'sconatus, Damasio'shomeostasis and somatic markers are not interchangeable constructs. The article distinguishes structural comparison from identity; do not add their labels as synonyms.
Clinical emotional deficits do not by themselves determine moral personhood, rights or responsibility. This philosophical account is not a validated clinical capacity test.

Correlations of moral outputs with humans do not prove a shared mechanism or agency, but behavioural evidence is not necessarily irrelevant to every competing account. Avoid treating underdetermination as proof of the author's preferred ontology.
The suggestion agent-type differences in human judgment may track a real asymmetry is a hypothesis, not proof those differences are unbiased or justified.
Responsibility returning to designers/deployers does not automatically solve foreseeability, control or collective accountability. No universal allocation of liability is derived.
Reports of low robustness in particular stress/dual-process studies are secondary. They do not refute every dual-process account or validate the author's alternative.
Broad novelty claims that two literatures have not theorized the distinction are not verified by a systematic literature search. Prior moral-zombie and functional-agency debates are themselves cited.

Original books, primary neuroscience, homeostatic-RL/robotics implementations and cited model experiments were not independently read or reproduced. No synthetic experimental result is created from their bibliography.

cross_paper_learning.finding: Schramowski measures model representations/outputs, not a self-maintaining moral subject. Gültekin's conceptual interpretation must not be imported as an empirical conclusion of that model study.

Almeida explicitly remains neutral about machine mental states while using psychological methods. The agreement-versus-mechanism distinction supports caution without establishing Gültekin's particular constitutive criterion.
Colombatto measures folk consciousness attribution. Those ratings, Gültekin's proposed agency criteria and actual phenomenal experience are distinct evidence layers.
Both conceptual papers insist on human/institutional responsibility, but their philosophical criteria are not settled legal rules or measurements of actual responsibility allocation.
Sociomorphism and perceived moral agency concern human interpretation. They cannot by themselves determine actual nonhuman capacities or moral status.

deferred.reason: A philosophical organizing concept, not a separately demonstrated behaviour or synonym for agent self-preservation. The cited Spinoza text was not independently read.

deferred.term: Homeostasis / endogenous valuation as new errors
deferred.reason: Regulatory organization and theoretical valuation conditions are not inherently erroneous behaviours. No extra IDs for each component of the author's criterion.
Author's critique of an operationalization, not an experimentally established independent cognitive mechanism.
A philosophical thought-experiment category, not an observable validated AI behaviour or consciousness finding.
Explicit predictions and proposed protocols, not results; retain in study notes for later testing.

limitations: Two clearly typed conceptual entries added: an author-proposed inference error and a secondary psychological hypothesis, not two validated AI mechanisms.
No empirical paper coverage inferred from proposed experiments or unread books; existing dual-process note is a noncorroborating conceptual reference.
